title: Xanthe and the Portrait
premise: Theo Halloran, a property surveyor with seven years of unexplained noises in his own flat, is hired to appraise Wrenfield House, where his sleep recordings begin capturing a second voice that answers questions he never asked aloud. The voice belongs to Edith Marsh, whose portrait was cut from its frame and stolen in 1974 by the house's then-caretaker—Theo's own grandfather—and the house will not release anyone, living or dead, until the portrait returns. As Theo uncovers his family's theft and the last resident, elderly solicitor Marguerite Voss, prepares to sign the sale papers that will seal the house's fate forever, he must choose between protecting his family's name and freeing a woman who has been trapped in paint for fifty years. In the end, Theo returns the portrait, Edith dissolves into peace as the house exhales its final breath, and Theo signs the papers himself—choosing truth over loyalty to the dead man who raised him.
about_author: Ivo Thackeray is the pen name of a former building inspector from coastal Yorkshire who spent a decade cataloguing structural defects in houses nobody wanted to buy. Their fiction blends surveyor's precision with the slow dread of places that remember more than their occupants do.

chapters.title: The House That Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Theo. He arrives at Wrenfield House for a routine appraisal and finds the rooms subtly rearranged between measurements. A cold professional beat: he tells himself it's settling timber, but the reader sees him flinch at a door he didn't open.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Flashback woven through present-day inspection. Theo recalls the noises in his own flat—footsteps above a top-floor ceiling, breathing behind plaster—and the rationalizations he built like scaffolding. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: Marguerite Voss, Last Resident
chapters.summary: POV alternates between Theo and Marguerite. The elderly solicitor shows him the house's deeds and mentions, casually, that she has lived alone since 1974 'except for her.' Theo assumes dementia; Marguerite knows better. Beat: two people lying politely to each other.

chapters.title: The Empty Frame
chapters.summary: Theo finds a life-sized empty frame bolted to the wall of the east bedroom, dust shaped around a missing canvas. The wallpaper behind it is unfaded—a perfect silhouette. Beat: first true fear, the sense of an absence with weight.

chapters.title: Sleep Recordings
chapters.summary: Theo, a lifelong insomniac, plays back his recorder from the night in the house. Between his own mutterings: a second voice, dry and patient, answering questions he doesn't remember asking. Beat: violation—the most private space breached.

chapters.title: 'What Did You Take?'
chapters.summary: He replays the tape obsessively. The voice asks HIM questions too: what did you take, who told you to come, do you look like him? Theo has no idea what any of it means yet. Beat: paranoia curdling into compulsion.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Warning
chapters.summary: Marguerite finds him listening to the recording and goes white. She tells him to finish the appraisal and leave before the equinox, refusing to explain. Beat: the first crack in her composure; Theo realizes she isn't senile—she's terrified.

chapters.title: Grandfather's Toolbox
chapters.summary: Sorting his late grandfather's effects for probate, Theo finds a toolbox with false bottom: newspaper clippings from 1974 about a theft at Wrenfield House, and a receipt signed H. Halloran. Beat: the floor drops out of his identity.

chapters.title: Edith Marsh, 1911–1974
chapters.summary: Research chapter, Theo's POV. Newspaper archives reveal Edith Marsh, the painter of the stolen portrait, who died the same week it vanished. Marguerite's sister-in-law, once. Beat: grief for a stranger; the past acquiring faces.

chapters.title: The Voice Has a Name
chapters.summary: That night in the house, Theo speaks aloud for the first time: 'Edith?' The recorder captures a long silence, then: 'Yes.' Beat: terror and strange relief—naming the thing makes it real and, somehow, less monstrous.

chapters.title: Questions at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: Structured as transcript fragments interleaved with Theo's waking dread. Edith answers questions about the house but not about how she died. She asks about his grandfather with something like hunger. Beat: intimacy forming across the impossible.

chapters.title: Loyalty to a Dead Man
chapters.summary: Theo confronts his memories of his grandfather—kind, careful, the man who raised him after his parents' death. The clippings don't fit the man he loved. Beat: loyalty vs. truth begins its real argument.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Saw
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, 1974 flashback. Young Marguerite watched her brother-in-law carry the wrapped canvas out at dawn and said nothing—for fifty years. Beat: guilt as architecture; her silence built the haunting.

chapters.title: The Appraisal Deadline
chapters.summary: Present day. The buyers' solicitors push to close before month's end; Marguerite must sign or lose everything. Theo realizes the sale date falls on the equinox Edith mentioned. Beat: clock starts ticking in earnest.

chapters.title: Rooms That Won't Measure
chapters.summary: Theo's instruments fail systematically in the east wing—laser readings return impossible numbers, photographs develop with the frame occupied by a smear of grey light. Beat: the rational toolkit breaking down.

chapters.title: Where Is the Portrait?
chapters.summary: Edith tells Theo, through the recordings, that she can feel the canvas—cold, folded, far away. His grandfather hid it somewhere. Theo begins searching his grandfather's old properties. Beat: quest structure ignites.

chapters.title: The Cottage in Saltburn
chapters.summary: Theo searches his grandfather's inherited cottage. Behind a boarded chimney he finds scratch marks and a child's drawing of a lady with no face—but no portrait. Someone got there first, or almost did. Beat: hope and frustration.

chapters.title: A Rival in the Records
chapters.summary: Theo discovers someone else has been asking about the 1974 theft: an antiques dealer named Corven who contacted Marguerite last spring. Marguerite admits she nearly sold information to him out of desperation. Beat: human greed enters the ghost story.

chapters.title: Corven
chapters.summary: Theo tracks down Corven, charming and wrong-eyed, who claims to know where the portrait is and offers to split its value. Something about him makes Edith's presence in the house go silent and cold when Theo mentions him. Beat: distrust established.

chapters.title: The Second Voice on the Tape
chapters.summary: Reviewing old recordings from his own flat, Theo hears Corven's cadence in a voice captured years ago—he's been near this before, longer than chance allows. Beat: the haunting retroactively colonizes Theo's whole adult life.

chapters.title: Marguerite Breaks
chapters.summary: Marguerite confesses fully: her brother-in-law Henry Halloran stole the portrait to pay debts, and Edith died chasing him down the drive—fell, struck her head, and the house took her into the frame's absence. Beat: the central secret lands; grief and fury.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Marguerite loved Edith; saying it aloud for the first time in fifty years costs her everything. She begs Theo not to find the portrait—not because it's dangerous, but because letting Edith go means finally being alone. Beat: the theme made flesh.

chapters.title: The House Turns
chapters.summary: With the sale nearing, the house stops being subtle: doors seal, the temperature drops, and every mirror shows the empty frame instead of reflections. Theo is effectively imprisoned inside overnight. Beat: escalation from eerie to hostile.

chapters.title: Night Inside
chapters.summary: Trapped, Theo talks to Edith through the dark. She admits she could keep him—could make him stay the way she stayed—if he doesn't help her. It is not a threat so much as a confession of desperation. Beat: sympathy and fear braided together.

chapters.title: Corven's Offer Again
chapters.summary: Corven appears at the house gates with a legal angle: he's representing the buyers and can delay closing if Theo helps him locate the portrait for 'authentication.' Theo realizes Corven intends to sell it, trapping Edith forever in private hands. Beat: stakes sharpen.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: In the house's estate records, Theo finds his grandfather's debt ledger and a final entry: 'Saltburn, under the floor where she stood.' Not the cottage—the boathouse. Beat: clue resolution; momentum surges.

chapters.title: Boathouse
chapters.summary: Theo pries up the boathouse floorboards at low tide and finds a oilskin-wrapped canvas, water-stained but intact: Edith's face looking out, painted by her own hand, alive even in pigment. Beat: awe—the object itself is uncanny.

chapters.title: What the Portrait Wants
chapters.summary: Back at the house, the portrait won't leave Theo's car—it reappears inside despite being locked away. Edith's voice is stronger now, clearer, and the house grows quieter wherever the canvas rests. Beat: the rules of the haunting revealed.

chapters.title: Corven Takes It
chapters.summary: Corven breaks into Theo's car and steals the portrait. Edith's voice vanishes mid-sentence, and the house's rage becomes immediate and physical—windows blowing inward, walls weeping cold brine. Beat: darkest hour.

chapters.title: Marguerite Signs
chapters.summary: Under pressure from the buyers, a defeated Marguerite signs the sale papers. The moment ink dries, the house begins to die—rooms folding in on themselves, the east bedroom going black. Beat: point of no return.

chapters.title: Chasing Corven
chapters.summary: Theo tracks Corven to a storage unit in Middlesbrough using the ledger's contacts list. Confrontation: Corven, cornered, reveals he's been hearing her too for months and is terrified—greed was armor. Beat: villain humanized, still dangerous.

chapters.title: The Bargain
chapters.summary: Theo offers Corven the one thing more valuable than the portrait: his testimony about the theft, clearing the Halloran name into infamy, if Corven returns the canvas untouched. Corven, hollowed out by fear, agrees. Beat: Theo pays the price loyalty demanded.

chapters.title: Return
chapters.summary: Equinox eve. Theo carries the portrait up the stairs of a dying house while Marguerite watches from the landing, unable to climb. The walls lean in like an audience. Beat: pilgrimage; every step costs something.

chapters.title: Restoration
chapters.summary: Theo sets the canvas back into the frame. For one moment the painted Edith looks at him—not at the room, at him—and the house inhales. Then the image begins to fade, taking her with it. Beat: climax's threshold.

chapters.title: Edith
chapters.summary: Final conversation, rendered as voice fading word by word. Edith forgives neither Henry nor herself entirely, but releases both. Her last words are to Marguerite, carried down the stairs: 'You kept me. That was enough.' Beat: catharsis.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: The house settles into ordinary ruin. Marguerite, weeping and lighter, tears up nothing—she lets the sale stand, choosing to finally leave the place that held her hostage to her own grief. Beat: love against duty resolved in her arc.

chapters.title: Papers
chapters.summary: Theo signs the appraisal honestly, noting structural failure beyond repair, killing the sale and preserving the house as a derelict trust in Edith's name. His career may suffer. Beat: truth chosen over safety, quietly.

chapters.title: Explanations, Finally
chapters.summary: Epilogue-adjacent: Theo plays his old flat recordings one last time and hears only his own breathing. Seven years of noises have stopped—or he has finally stopped needing them explained. Beat: memory laid to rest.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Theo visits his grandfather's grave and tells him, aloud, what he did and what it cost. He leaves the debt ledger on the stone. Beat: loyalty transformed—honoring the man by refusing his lie.

chapters.title: Wrenfield, Empty
chapters.summary: Closing chapter, quiet and observational. Theo drives past Wrenfield House one year later; it stands open to sky, unhaunted, just old. In his pocket, a photograph of the empty frame, which he keeps not as evidence but as remembrance. Beat: peace earned, memory preserved.
